evidence.fitness: A researcher can build on it: pinned commit, committed rows with attribution, deterministic seeded runs, stdlib. But nearest prior work is not cited or compared: Schmidt, Melchior, Hawkes and Staffell 2019 (Joule 3:81) publish exactly this map (cheapest technology by discharge duration and cycles, with Monte Carlo cost uncertainty, 2015-2050), and Viswanathan et al. 2022 (PNNL-33283), the source of four of the five cost sets, publishes its own LCOS by technology and duration that the project never compares against. Novelty is a reanalysis of PNNL/DEA inputs through a 90-line model; not the PhD-level programme research/CLAUDE.md asks for.
evidence.domain: Compared against Schmidt et al. 2019 / Lazard LCOS practice. Departures an analyst hits in the first hour: (1) blocks with lives shorter than the project are not replaced; instead the project life is the capital-weighted mean of block lives (sourced.py:81), so the Li-ion inverter (10 y) and the fuel cell (10 y, inside a 54.6 y weighted life at 500 h) are amortised over the wrong period; replacing the Li-ion inverter at year 10 raises 4 h LCOS from 120.6 to 130.4 $/MWh (margin over CAES 134 shrinks from 13 to 4), and per-block annuitisation raises hydrogen 500 h from 425 to 496 (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/27f32908-f8a8-5080-a56e-0c9dfcf6bcdb/scratchpad/recompute.py); (2) Li-ion RTE taken as 0.96^2 although the source value is a DC round trip (AC-AC for LFP is nearer 0.85-0.88, NREL ATB uses 0.85); (3) no end-of-life cost or construction period; (4) the 2,000 h/yr discharge budget is not a market-derived dispatch. Point-estimate winners survive these; Monte Carlo shares at 4-10 h would move toward CAES/PSH.

Inverter replacement at y10 moves Li-ion 4 h from $121 to $130/MWh (margin over CAES $134 shrinks from 13 to 4); per-block annuitisation moves hydrogen 500 h from $425 to $496. Point winners hold; Monte Carlo shares at 4-10 h are biased toward Li-ion.

DEA battery-inverter efficiency 0.96 is labelled upstream ':  Round trip efficiency DC' but the README calls it '96% one way' and the code squares it to RTE 0.9216; the 'sourced' Li-ion efficiency misreads its source (LCOS effect ~1.3 $/MWh at 4 h; an AC-AC figure would be lower still).
Zeroing the ATB pumped-hydro site-class spread (which drives the headline '8 h: pumped hydro 52%') leaves all 10 tests green; no test pins a headline LCOS or win share.

Nearest prior work not cited or compared: Schmidt et al. 2019 (Joule) publish the same cheapest-technology-by-duration map with Monte Carlo, and PNNL-33283 (source of four cost sets) publishes its own LCOS by duration; novelty is a reanalysis through a simple model.

verdict: Does not meet the bar (verification 2, claims 2, median 2); finished (completeness 3). The arithmetic is sound: five headline LCOS values recompute to within rounding from the upstream technology-data file with an independent script, and both experiment scripts reproduce byte-identically. What a storage techno-economic analyst would reject is the method around the numbers: short-lived blocks (Li-ion inverter, fuel cell) are averaged into a capital-weighted life instead of replaced, which understates Li-ion 4 h by ~8% and hydrogen 500 h by ~17%; the Li-ion efficiency misreads a DC round-trip figure as one-way; the PSH spread behind the 52% headline is untested; and Schmidt et al. 2019 and PNNL's own LCOS, the obvious comparisons, are absent. Point-estimate winners survive all of these.
